newsitem.title: TAIWAN: New data fuel Taiwan hopes for gathering recovery.
newsitem.headline: New data fuel Taiwan hopes for gathering recovery.

text.p: Taiwan on Tuesday reported slightly higher than expected growth in export orders and industrial output in January, bolstering economists' view that a stable but slow recovery has taken root.
Foreign orders for Taiwan goods rose 2.03 percent to US$9.872 billion in January compared to January 1996, the Economics Ministry said on Tuesday.
The official January export order figure was slightly higher than the average forecast of 1.58 percent that resulted from a February 14 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.

January's industrial output rose an annual 6.01 percent compared to January 1996, the ministry said. The official industrial output figure was nearly a full percentage point higher than the average forecast of 5.02 percent that resulted from the February 14 Reuters Poll.
Taiwan's higher-than-expected 6.62 percent fourth quarter gross domestic product growth announced last week brought new cheer to an island that still relies heavily on exports.
The uptick prompted Taiwan's statistics agency to boost its forecast for 1997 GDP growth to 6.28 percent from 6.20 percent, compared to with the actual 5.71 percent growth in 1996.
"With the two latest data, we can say the recovery is for sure now, but in a slow pace," said HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang.

"Both figures were slightly better than expected," Wang said. "But still, they fell into expectations that the first quarter economic performance will be weaker than the hot-sale season in the fourth quarter of last year."
National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang noted that Taiwan's sizzling stock market gained new steam from the strong fourth-quarter and January economic indicators.
"The current situation is still showing signs of a gradual recovery," Lin said.

At US$9.87 billion, January export orders were below the US$10 billion-plus levels clocked in each of the previous five months, while industrial output was 2.74 percent below that of December, the ministry said.

Economists said they expected slow growth for export orders in 1997, but higher and stable growth for industrial output due to growing domestic demand fuelled by likely rises in private investment, private consumption and government investment.

"Exports and export orders this year should see slow growth of less than five percent, but we can see industrial output grow at more than five percent due to rising domestic demand," said Grand Cathay Securities vice-president Terry Chen.

The government statistics agency last week forecast Taiwan's private investment would rise 11 percent in 1997, while private consumption would grow 6.6 percent and government investment would rise 5.3 percent.

In January, export orders from Hong Kong -- including indirect trade with rival China -- fell a year-on-year 7.12 percent. Economists said this was related to China's setting a December 31 deadline for the cancellation of tax-free treatment on equipment imports by foreign investors.
"Taiwan investors in the mainland therefore increased their machinery imports from Taiwan to beat the deadline, resulting in relatively weaker imports from Taiwan in January," Chen said.
